title: Fast Distributed Inference Serving for Large Language Models
technique: token-level preemptive scheduling with skip-join Multi-Level Feedback Queue + proactive KV-cache swap between GPU and host

optimized_metrics.evidence: use preemptive scheduling to eliminate head-of-line blocking problem and minimize latency
optimized_metrics.stat_quote: although FastServe is designed to reduce average latency; average per-token latency is calculated as the mean of every job's end-to-end latency divided by its output length

optimized_metrics.evidence: we want the maximum throughput as high as possible under a certain latency requirement

headline_claim.text: compared to the state-of-the-art solution vLLM, FastServe improves the throughput by up to 31.4x and 17.9x under the same average and tail latency requirements, respectively

reported_metrics.where: headline only (re-pass); tail-audit: E2E not a separate target, duplicates NORM_LAT mean
headline only (re-pass); tail-audit: P95 goodput is an evaluation metric, not a design target

metric_definitions.definition_quote: average per-token latency is calculated as the mean of every job's end-to-end latency divided by its output length.
metric_definitions.notes: normalized by output length only; includes queueing; mean over jobs

metric_definitions.definition_quote: In addition, we also report the P95 tail latency.
metric_definitions.notes: P95 of the same per-token (normalized) latency, presumably; not stated whether normalized

metric_definitions.definition_quote: we measure the P95 goodput, defined as the throughput when 95% of jobs can be completed within the SLO of the initialization phase and the decoding phase.
metric_definitions.notes: two-phase SLO (initialization/prefill and decoding); SLO = 5x/10x/20x the latency of the phase under light load

metric_definitions.definition_quote: compare the maximum throughput each system can achieve under the SLO
metric_definitions.notes: throughput is the max request rate (req/s) sustained under the latency SLO; unit not explicitly defined

slo_spec: Latency SLO set to 10x the latency of a single decoding iteration (= 0.3 s based on profiling) for latency curves; for goodput, SLO of both phases = 5x/10x/20x of the per-phase latency under light load; starvation threshold alpha tuned from user SLO (default 300 ms).
load_regime: Poisson request-rate sweep; ShareGPT and Alpaca; also a fixed-length synthetic workload
tradeoff_acknowledged: preemption may hurt tail latency of long jobs (mitigated by starvation prevention); paper says tail latency improved too
hardware: NVIDIA A100 GPUs (up to 16 for OPT-175B)
extractor_notes: 'Latency' in the headline is per-token normalized latency (e2e/output length) while 'throughput' is request throughput at an SLO on that latency; the SLO is a latency threshold of 0.3 s on the per-token measure (inferred). Goodput is also reported. | TAIL AUDIT 2026-10-06: E2E tail stat -> n/a (metric targeted, percentile only reported)

tail_audit.metrics: E2E/NORM_LAT mean (target); P95 latency + P95 goodput (reported/eval)
tail_audit.correction: Demote E2E P95 'objective' to reported. GOODPUT P95 is an evaluation metric (throughput at which 95% of jobs meet SLO), not a design target; the scheduler minimizes mean JCT (skip-join MLFQ). Keep NORM_LAT mean + THR_REQ under latency requirement.

load_class_quote: request arrival ... generated using a Poisson process parameterized by the arrival rate (§6.1); latency vs request rate curves (Fig 11-12)
repass_log: NORM_LAT: abstract quote replaced by §1 design statement; stat mean now explicit ('designed to reduce average latency')
E2E: moved to reported (result-only abstract quote; tail-audit correction)
GOODPUT P95: moved to reported (tail-audit correction: evaluation metric)
